content.name: ʾālep
content.sound: a glottal stop (the catch in "uh-oh"); Greeks used it for the vowel A
content.notes: Turn the Latin A upside down and you can still see the horns of the ox.
traditions: Revelation 1:8 and 22:13: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end."
In Sefer Yetzirah, Aleph is one of the three "mother letters" and is linked with air. Aleph is silent, which later writers read as a sign of the One God.
Alif opens the letter groups of several surahs (Alif Lam Mim, Quran 2:1). Their meaning is not explained in the Quran; tradition says "God knows best".

content.name: bēt
content.notes: "Alphabet" is simply the first two Greek letters, alpha + beta. Hebrew place names like Bethlehem ("house of bread") and Bethel ("house of God") still carry the word.
traditions: The Torah begins with Bet (Bereshit, "In the beginning"). Midrash asks why it does not begin with Aleph and gives several teaching answers.

content.name: gīml
content.picture: perhaps a throwing stick or a boomerang-like hunting tool
content.notes: Etruscans had no g sound, so the Romans used C for both k and g. About 230 BC a new letter G was made by adding a stroke to C (traditionally credited to Spurius Carvilius Ruga).
traditions: The Talmud (Shabbat 104a) reads Gimel and Dalet as "gemol dalim", give to the poor.

content.name: dālet
content.notes: The Greek capital Δ gave its name to the triangular mouth of a river, the Nile delta.

content.name: hē
content.meaning: window, or a shout of joy (debated)
content.picture: a man with raised arms, rejoicing or praying (Egyptian sign A28)
content.notes: Greeks needed vowels, so they turned this breathy h into the vowel E. Later Byzantines called it e-psilon, "bare e".
traditions: He stands for the name of God in short (often written ה׳ in print). Genesis 17 adds a He to Abram and Sarai, making Abraham and Sarah.

content.name: wāw
content.notes: One Phoenician letter gave Latin five: F (from the Greek digamma), and U, V, W and Y (from upsilon). U and V were the same letter until the 1500s-1600s; W began as a doubled u/v in the early Middle Ages.
traditions: Vav is also the word "hook"; the hooks of the Tabernacle curtains are vavim (Exodus 26:32). As a prefix it means "and".

content.name: zayin
content.picture: perhaps a weapon or a manacle
content.notes: Latin dropped Z early, then borrowed it back from Greek in the 1st century BC for Greek words. That is why it sits at the very end.

content.name: ḥēt
content.sound: a rough h (ch as in Bach)
content.notes: In Greek it became the long vowel E (eta); in Latin it stayed a consonant, H.
traditions: Chet + Yod spell chai, "life", worth 8 + 10 = 18. Gifts in multiples of 18 are a custom.

content.name: ṭēt
content.notes: Theta keeps the round shape. Latin had no use for it.

content.name: yōd
content.notes: The smallest Hebrew letter: the "jot" of Matthew 5:18 is the Greek iota, standing for yod. J split off from I in the 1500s (Gian Giorgio Trissino argued for separate letters in 1524).
traditions: Matthew 5:18: "one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law".
Yod begins the four-letter divine name YHWH.

content.name: kap
content.notes: Latin mostly used C for k, keeping K for a few words like Kalendae.

content.name: lāmed
content.picture: an ox goad or shepherd's crook
content.notes: Lamed is the tallest Hebrew letter. The word comes from l-m-d, "to teach" (a goad trains oxen).
traditions: Talmud students (lamdan) and the verb "to learn" share the root of Lamed.

content.name: mēm
content.notes: The zigzag of water waves is still in the shape of M.
traditions: In Sefer Yetzirah, Mem is a "mother letter" linked with water.
Mim closes the letter group Alif Lam Mim that opens surahs 2, 3, 29, 30, 31 and 32.

content.name: nūn
content.notes: Joshua was "son of Nun". In Aramaic nun means fish, which later readers connected with the letter.
traditions: Surah 68 opens with the single letter Nun ("Nun. By the pen...").

content.name: sāmek
content.picture: perhaps a pillar or a fish skeleton
content.notes: The history of X is tangled: Latin X comes from a western Greek form, not straight from samekh.

content.name: ʿayin
content.sound: a throat sound unknown in English
content.notes: Greeks kept the round eye and made it a vowel, O. Ayin also means "spring of water" in Hebrew place names (En-gedi).

content.name: pē
content.notes: Greek pi became the famous circle number (first used for it by William Jones, 1706).

content.name: ṣādē
content.picture: perhaps a plant or a hook
content.notes: Greek used it briefly as the letter san, and kept a form as the number sign sampi (900).
traditions: Surah 38 opens with the single letter Sad.

content.name: qōp
content.meaning: eye of a needle, back of the head, or monkey (debated)
content.sound: q (k made far back in the throat)
content.notes: Greek dropped koppa as a letter but kept it as the number 90. Latin kept it as Q, almost always before U.
traditions: Surah 50 opens with the single letter Qaf.

content.name: rēš
content.notes: Latin added a tail to the Greek P (rho) to tell R apart from P.
traditions: Rosh Hashanah, "head of the year", uses the same word, rosh.

content.name: šīn
content.cyrillic: С, Ш (Ш probably from Hebrew shin)
content.notes: Greek turned it on its side as sigma (Σ).
traditions: Shin is on the mezuzah case, standing for Shaddai (Almighty). In Sefer Yetzirah it is a "mother letter" linked with fire.

content.name: tāw
content.notes: The last Phoenician letter. In Ezekiel 9:4 a "mark" (Hebrew tav) is put on foreheads; in the old script that mark was an X or +.
traditions: Tav is the last letter, so "from Aleph to Tav" means from beginning to end; emet, truth, starts with the first letter and ends with the last.
Early Christians linked the tau-shaped mark of Ezekiel 9:4 with the cross.

items.title: GREEK_ADDED: Υ υ
content: Greek development of waw; gave Latin Y, and U/V/W

items.title: GREEK_ADDED: Χ χ
content: A Greek addition; in western Greek it stood for ks and gave Latin X

items.title: GREEK_ADDED: Ω ω
content: "Big O", a Greek addition for long o; "Alpha and Omega" = first and last

items.title: LATIN_LATER: G
content: C with a stroke, so g and k could be told apart

items.title: LATIN_LATER: Y, Z
content: borrowed back from Greek for Greek words, so they went to the end

items.title: LATIN_LATER: W
content: a doubled u/v ("double u"), first in Old English and German writing

items.title: LATIN_LATER: J
content: split off from I; Trissino argued for it in 1524

items.title: LATIN_LATER: U / V
content: one letter until printers began using V for the consonant and U for the vowel

items.title: RUNES: ᛈ
content: unknown (perhaps a pear tree or a game)

items.title: STORY: -3200
content: Egyptian hieroglyphs and Sumerian cuneiform: writing with hundreds of signs.

items.title: STORY: -1850
content: Proto-Sinaitic: workers in the Sinai turquoise mines use Egyptian pictures for single sounds (the first alphabet, as most scholars see it).

items.title: STORY: -1400
content: Ugarit writes a 30-letter alphabet in cuneiform wedges.

items.title: STORY: -1050
content: Phoenician: 22 letters, all consonants, written right to left, carried by traders around the Mediterranean.

items.title: STORY: -800
content: Greek: borrows the letters and turns some into vowels (A, E, I, O, Y). Paleo-Hebrew and Aramaic grow from the same Phoenician letters.

items.title: STORY: -700
content: Etruscans take a western Greek alphabet; Romans take theirs from the Etruscans.

items.title: STORY: -500
content: Aramaic becomes the script of the Persian Empire; the Hebrew "square" letters grow from it.

items.title: STORY: 150
content: Runes (Elder Futhark) appear in northern Europe, probably adapted from an Old Italic alphabet.

items.title: STORY: 400
content: Arabic script develops from Nabataean Aramaic (earliest Arabic inscriptions 4th-6th centuries).

items.title: STORY: 863
content: Glagolitic script for Slavic (Cyril and Methodius); Cyrillic follows in Bulgaria about 900.

items.title: STORY: 1524
content: Trissino argues for J and U as separate letters.

items.title: EXTRA: Medina
content: Yathrib; Muhammad moved here in 622 (the Hijra).

items.title: EXTRA: Ugarit
content: Ras Shamra; Bronze Age city with early alphabetic tablets.

items.title: EXTRA: Mari
content: Tell Hariri; royal archives of about 25,000 tablets.

items.title: EXTRA: Ebla
content: Tell Mardikh; archive of about 17,000 tablets.

items.title: EXTRA: Persepolis
content: Ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire.

items.title: EXTRA: Rosetta
content: Rashid; where the Rosetta Stone was found (1799).

items.title: EXTRA: Aksum
content: Ancient Ethiopian kingdom; Ge'ez Enoch and Jubilees survived here.

items.title: ANY_PAINTING: First look
content: Before reading the label: where does your eye land first, where does it go next, and where does it rest? Name one feeling in a single word.

items.title: ANY_PAINTING: Composition
content: Find the main shapes: triangle, diagonal, circle, horizon. What is in the centre, what is pushed to the edge? Is it calm (horizontals and verticals) or restless (diagonals)?

items.title: ANY_PAINTING: Light & colour
content: Where is the light coming from, and what does it pick out? Which colour is strongest? Warm colours come forward, cool ones recede.

items.title: ANY_PAINTING: Symbols & details
content: Look at hands, objects, animals, flowers and what lies on tables or floors. Small things were often placed on purpose (see the Symbols guide).

items.title: ANY_PAINTING: The artist & the time
content: When and where was it made, and who paid for it: a church, a king, a merchant, the artist alone? Who was meant to see it?

items.title: ANY_PAINTING: What it meant
content: What did it say to people then, and what does it say to you now? What is left out?

items.title: ANY_PAINTING: Strategist's read
content: What does this tell you about what its makers valued, feared and wanted others to believe?

items.title: GALLERY: Young Woman with a Water Pitcher

content.title: Young Woman with a Water Pitcher
content.q: Vermeer Young Woman with a Water Pitcher
content.look: The eye goes to her face and hand at the window, then down to the gleaming silver basin and pitcher.
content.composition: A still rectangle of verticals and horizontals: window, map, table edge. Nothing moves except the moment of opening the window.
content.light: Cool daylight from the left (Vermeer’s usual window) falls across the white headdress; blue and white dominate, with the ultramarine in the cloth.
content.symbols: The map on the wall shows the world of Dutch trade; the silver pitcher and basin were for washing and stood for purity and a well-run household.
content.context: Vermeer worked slowly in Delft, painting only about 35 surviving pictures. The Dutch Republic was the richest trading state in Europe and its merchants bought paintings of ordinary rooms.
content.meaning: A quiet ideal of order, cleanliness and prosperity: the home as a small, calm republic.
content.strategist: A trading people who prized order, privacy and wealth earned by commerce, not by conquest or kings. Expect them to negotiate for markets and stability, and to fight hard for their sea lanes.

content.title: The Harvesters
content.look: The golden wheat field fills the left; the eye then drops to the workers eating under the pear tree and travels out across the valley to a far harbour.
content.composition: A strong diagonal of cut wheat leads from the foreground into a deep landscape. The tree trunk divides near work from the wide world.
content.light: Hot late-summer light, ochres and golds against blue-green distance (aerial perspective).
content.symbols: Wheat and harvest stand for the cycle of the year; one man sleeps sprawled under the tree, the rest eat together, others still cut.
content.context: One of six paintings of the times of year made for Niclaes Jongelinck, a rich Antwerp merchant, for his house. Five survive.
content.meaning: Ordinary peasants as the heroes of a whole season: labour, rest and food as the rhythm of life.
content.strategist: A society that ran on harvests and trade, whose rich patrons enjoyed seeing the land and labour that fed them. Bread and the seasons set the limits of every campaign.

items.title: GALLERY: Aristotle with a Bust of Homer

content.title: Aristotle with a Bust of Homer
content.q: Rembrandt Aristotle with a Bust of Homer
content.look: Light on Aristotle’s face and sleeve, then his hand resting on the white bust of Homer, then the gold chain.
content.composition: A triangle from the bust up to the face and down to the chain: thought, wisdom of the past, and worldly reward linked together.
content.light: Rembrandt’s deep shadow and warm golden light (chiaroscuro); the black hat and dark background push the thinking face forward.
content.symbols: The gold chain carries a medal of Alexander the Great, Aristotle’s pupil: a reward from power. The blind poet Homer stands for pure art and wisdom.
content.context: Commissioned by Don Antonio Ruffo, a Sicilian nobleman and collector. Rembrandt was famous but heading towards bankruptcy (1656).
content.meaning: A philosopher weighing fame and favour from rulers against the lasting value of wisdom and art.
content.strategist: A culture that respected learning and individual conscience, and was uneasy about how power buys thinkers. Reputation mattered; flattery did not fully convince.

content.title: The Death of Socrates
content.look: Socrates, lit and upright, points upward while reaching for the cup of hemlock. Then the grieving followers, then Plato slumped at the foot of the bed.
content.composition: A frieze like an ancient relief, figures in a row parallel to the picture. The calm verticals of Socrates contrast with the collapsing curves of his friends.
content.light: Hard, clear light like a stage; sharp outlines and strong reds and blues.
content.symbols: The raised finger: his mind is on ideas and principle, not on death. Discarded chains on the floor. The man handing over the cup hides his face.
content.context: Painted two years before the French Revolution. Enlightenment Paris admired Roman and Greek virtue as a lesson against a corrupt court.
content.meaning: Dying for principle rather than giving up the truth. It became a model for revolutionary heroism.
content.strategist: A society on the edge of revolution, whose educated class glorified self-sacrifice for ideas. Leaders who believe this are hard to bribe and hard to frighten, and may welcome martyrdom.

content.title: Washington Crossing the Delaware
content.look: Washington standing in the boat against the brightening sky; then the flag; then the men rowing through the ice.
content.composition: A strong diagonal of boats crossing left to right (forward, into the future). Washington is the peak of a triangle of men.
content.light: Dawn breaking behind the leader: hope after the dark. Cold blues and whites, with red accents.
content.symbols: The flag shown is the Stars and Stripes, which did not exist yet in December 1776. The men are a mixed crew (a farmer, a frontiersman, a Black sailor, a Scot): the young nation in one boat.
content.context: Painted 75 years later by a German-American in Düsseldorf, to inspire European liberals after the failed revolutions of 1848.
content.meaning: A national legend, not a record: the real crossing was at night, in a storm. Painting history means shaping memory.
content.strategist: A young republic that told its story as courage against odds and unity of different people under one leader. Its legends show what it will rally around.

items.title: GALLERY: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave)

content.title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave)
content.q: Hokusai Under the Wave off Kanagawa
content.look: The great claw of the wave at the top left, then down to the boats, then across to tiny Mount Fuji in the hollow.
content.composition: The wave’s curve frames Fuji; the enormous near wave makes the sacred mountain look small. It reads right to left, the Japanese reading direction.
content.light: Flat colour from woodblocks, led by imported Prussian blue, a new synthetic pigment then.
content.symbols: Fuji is the still centre, the wave is nature’s force, the oarsmen bend together to survive it.
content.context: One of the Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, printed in thousands of cheap copies for townspeople during the Edo period, when Japan was mostly closed to foreigners.
content.meaning: Human effort, enduring nature and a calm centre: later it shaped Van Gogh, Debussy and modern design.
content.strategist: A people who admired discipline under pressure and the long patience of the mountain. Expect teamwork and endurance; never mistake stillness for weakness.

content.title: Wheat Field with Cypresses
content.q: Van Gogh Wheat Field with Cypresses
content.look: The dark flame of the cypresses on the right, then the yellow wheat, then the curling clouds.
content.composition: Three bands: field, hills, sky. Everything moves in curves, even the ground.
content.light: Thick paint (impasto); yellow wheat against blue sky, the complementary colours he loved.
content.symbols: Cypresses were trees of graveyards and eternity in the south of France; wheat was his sign of the cycle of life.
content.context: Painted while he lived voluntarily at the asylum in Saint-Rémy, a year before his death.
content.meaning: Nature alive with energy; calm and turmoil in the same view.
content.strategist: The modern artist as an individual voice: the art no longer serves a king or church, which tells you power in that society had spread out.

items.title: GALLERY: View from Mount Holyoke, after a Thunderstorm (The Oxbow)

content.title: View from Mount Holyoke, after a Thunderstorm (The Oxbow)
content.look: The storm on the left, then the bright river bend on the right, then (look closely) the tiny painter at his easel.
content.composition: Split in two by a diagonal: wild, stormy wilderness on the left, tamed farmland on the right.
content.light: Dark storm clouds giving way to sunlit fields.
content.symbols: Some see the Hebrew letters for "Noah" cut into the far hillside, and read it upside down as "Shaddai" (the Almighty): God’s view of the land.
content.context: Cole worried that America’s wilderness was being destroyed by settlement and industry.
content.meaning: A choice facing a nation: wild nature or progress, and what is lost in between.
content.strategist: A nation conscious of its land as destiny and resource. Its art debated expansion itself.

content.title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
content.look: The couple walking toward you on the right, then the green lamp-post dividing the picture, then the wide new street behind.
content.composition: The lamp-post and its shadow cut the canvas in half; strong perspective lines of Haussmann’s new boulevards.
content.symbols: Umbrellas and fashionable dress: the new middle class; everyone near, no one connected.
content.context: Paris had just been rebuilt by Baron Haussmann with wide avenues (also easier for troops to move through).
content.meaning: Modern city life: elegant, orderly, a little lonely.
content.strategist: A state that rebuilt its capital for traffic, control and display. Its citizens look prosperous and separate: power here is administrative, not personal.

items.title: GALLERY: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884

content.title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884
content.q: Seurat Sunday on La Grande Jatte
content.look: The tall couple on the right in profile, then the girl in white in the centre, then the river.
content.composition: Stiff figures in rows, like an ancient frieze; very still for a holiday scene.
content.light: Tiny dots of pure colour that mix in your eye, based on the colour science of his day.
content.symbols: The monkey on a leash next to the elegant lady was a joke about loose morals; people of different classes share the park but never meet.
content.context: Seurat spent two years on it, doing dozens of studies on the island in the Seine.
content.meaning: Leisure as order and science: the modern city at rest.
content.strategist: A society that believed in method and science even in art. Its classes mix in public but keep their distance.

content.title: Juan de Pareja
content.look: Straight to his eyes: he looks back at you with dignity.
content.composition: A simple bust-length portrait; the body turned, the head to us.
content.light: Warm, soft light on the face; the background plain.
content.symbols: The fine lace collar was a sign of status. Pareja was then enslaved and Velázquez’s assistant.
content.context: Painted in Rome; shown at the Pantheon to great praise. Velázquez freed Pareja that year (contract 1650, in force 1654); Pareja became a painter himself.
content.meaning: A portrait that gives full human dignity to a man the law did not treat as free.
content.strategist: A court society built on rank, where talent could still win recognition. Status was visible in clothes; character in the face.

content.title: Night-Shining White
content.look: The horse rearing against its post, then the many red seals around it.
content.composition: A single horse, tethered, full of energy pulling against restraint.
content.light: Ink on paper; no shadows: the line carries the life.
content.symbols: The horse was the emperor’s favourite charger. The red stamps are seals and notes added by collectors and emperors over 1,200 years: its history is written on it.
content.context: Painted for Emperor Xuanzong, whose court loved horses from Central Asia; they meant military power.
content.meaning: Power that is strong but held in check by order.
content.strategist: An empire that valued disciplined strength, cavalry, and a written record of ownership and judgement passing through generations.

content.title: Human-headed winged lion (lamassu)
content.look: The bearded human face in the horned cap, then the wings, then the legs.
content.composition: Built into a doorway; from the front it stands still, from the side it strides.
content.light: Stone relief, once painted, lit by daylight at the palace gate.
content.symbols: It has five legs, so it looks complete from the front and from the side. The horned cap marks divine power. Guardians like it protected palace doors.
content.context: Ashurnasirpal II built a new capital at Nimrud and covered it with reliefs of his wars and hunts.
content.meaning: Power at the door: anyone entering felt the king’s strength before seeing him.
content.strategist: An empire that ruled by awe and fear. Its art was a warning to visitors and vassals. Expect shows of force and harsh punishment for revolt.

content.title: Hippopotamus ("William")
content.look: The bright blue body, then the plants drawn on it.
content.composition: A small solid figure on four short legs.
content.light: Blue-green glazed faience, the colour of the Nile.
content.symbols: Lotus flowers and river plants are painted on its skin: the hippo in its marsh. Three legs were deliberately broken in ancient times so the dangerous animal could not harm the dead.
content.context: Found in a tomb; hippos were feared river animals that overturned boats.
content.meaning: Protection and the forces of the Nile, tamed by art.
content.strategist: A civilisation organised around the river and the long view of eternity: careful, ordered, thinking in centuries.

items.title: GALLERY: The Burning of the Houses of Lords and Commons, 16 October 1834

content.title: The Burning of the Houses of Lords and Commons, 16 October 1834
content.q: Turner Burning of the Houses of Lords and Commons
content.look: The blaze across the river, then its reflection, then the crowds on the bridge and shore.
content.composition: Fire and its reflection form a great column of light; the bridge leads the eye into it.
content.light: Turner’s blazing yellows and reds dissolving into smoke and water.
content.symbols: The seat of government in flames, watched by thousands of ordinary Londoners.
content.context: Turner watched the real fire. It came two years after the Great Reform Act of 1832 changed who could vote.
content.meaning: An old order going up in smoke: drama, awe and change.
content.strategist: A society that could lose its parliament building and carry on: institutions mattered more than the stones.

items.title: GALLERY: Marble statue of a kouros (youth)

content.title: Marble statue of a kouros (youth)
content.look: The whole upright body, then the face, then the left foot set forward.
content.composition: Strict symmetry; arms at the sides, fists closed, weight on both legs.
content.symbols: The stance comes from Egyptian statues; the left foot forward. Greek sculptors would later learn to shift the weight (contrapposto).
content.context: Marked the grave of a young Athenian aristocrat.
content.meaning: The ideal young citizen: disciplined, balanced, beautiful.
content.strategist: A city that trained its young men to an ideal of body and discipline, and honoured them in public.

items.title: GALLERY: Fur Traders Descending the Missouri

content.title: Fur Traders Descending the Missouri
content.q: Bingham Fur Traders Descending the Missouri
content.look: The dark animal at the prow staring at you, then the old trader and his son, then the misty river.
content.composition: A flat triangle in a calm horizontal band; perfect stillness.
content.symbols: The animal (a bear cub or cat) is chained; the trader’s son is of mixed French and Native American descent, as many in the trade were.
content.context: The fur trade was ending as settlement moved west.
content.meaning: A calm, nostalgic picture of a frontier way of life that was disappearing.
content.strategist: A nation already romanticising its frontier while it changed it.

content.name: Ancient Egypt
content.honours: order (ma’at), the king as guarantor of order, continuity, the afterlife
content.fears: chaos, the desert, the river turning against them, being forgotten
content.power: the pharaoh shown largest, calm and unchanging; enemies small and bound
content.individual: the individual lives inside a fixed order; style hardly changed for 3,000 years
content.others: foreigners shown as bound captives on footstools and sandals
content.read: A people who planned in centuries and valued stability above novelty. Patient, bureaucratic, hard to rush; change comes slowly and must look like tradition.

content.name: Assyria
content.honours: the king’s strength, victory, the hunt
content.power: palace reliefs of sieges, deportations and lion hunts; guardian lamassu at the gates
content.individual: only the king is an individual; soldiers and enemies are repeated types
content.others: conquered peoples shown punished in detail, as a warning to visitors
content.read: Rule by terror and display. Strong, but brittle: hated by its subjects, it fell quickly when they united in 612 BC.

content.name: Classical Greece
content.honours: the ideal human body, balance, reason, the citizen
content.fears: hubris (pride that the gods punish), tyranny, disorder
content.power: gods and athletes as ideal humans; public statues paid for by the city
content.individual: growing: from stiff kouroi to relaxed contrapposto and personal portraits
content.others: outsiders as "barbarians" in battle friezes (Centaurs, Persians, Amazons)
content.read: Competitive city-states that prized excellence, debate and proportion. Expect argument, pride and alliances that shift.

content.name: Rome
content.honours: family, duty, law, the state; realistic portraits of elders (verism)
content.fears: civil war, loss of dignity, being forgotten
content.power: triumphal arches, coins with the emperor’s face, portraits in every province
content.individual: strong individual portraits, but always as servants of Rome
content.others: conquered peoples on coins and columns: defeated, then absorbed as citizens
content.read: Practical builders who conquered and then absorbed: they paid for loyalty with roads, law and citizenship.

content.name: Tang China
content.honours: harmony, scholarship, horses, a cosmopolitan court
content.power: horses, tomb figures of foreign traders, collectors’ seals marking authority
content.individual: the emperor and the scholar-official; art judged by brushwork and lineage
content.others: foreign merchants and musicians shown with curiosity in tomb figures
content.read: A confident empire open to trade, governing through officials and written records. Respect for precedent and long memory.

content.name: Edo Japan
content.honours: discipline, the seasons, craft, the floating world of city pleasures
content.power: the shogun kept peace through strict rank; prints were cheap art for townspeople
content.individual: actors and beauties as stars; the artist’s name mattered
content.others: Japan was mostly closed; Dutch traders were the window on Europe
content.read: Order maintained by rules and ritualised courtesy; great patience and endurance, and a love of refined craft.

content.name: Sixteenth-century Netherlands
content.honours: the land, work, everyday life, proverbs and moral lessons
content.fears: war and religious conflict (the Dutch Revolt began in 1568), hunger
content.power: merchants as patrons; peasants as subjects of art for the first time
content.individual: crowds of ordinary people, each doing something
content.others: Spanish rule was foreign rule, soon resisted
content.read: Merchant cities that watched everything closely and valued practical wisdom.

content.name: Dutch Golden Age
content.honours: trade, cleanliness, the home, science, sober dress
content.fears: vanity, the sea, losing wealth (still lifes with skulls warn against pride)
content.power: merchants and guilds, not kings, bought most of the art
content.individual: portraits of ordinary burghers; Rembrandt’s self-portraits
content.others: maps and globes everywhere: a world to trade with
content.read: A republic of traders: careful with money, proud of independence, fierce at sea. Negotiate on interests and contracts.

content.name: Spanish Golden Age
content.honours: faith, honour, rank, the royal court
content.power: court portraits of the Habsburg kings; Velázquez as court painter
content.individual: deep psychological portraits, from kings to dwarfs and servants
content.others: a global empire, Americas to the Philippines
content.read: An empire where honour and status rule decisions; pride can outweigh cost.

content.name: France before the Revolution
content.honours: reason, virtue, the ancient republics (in the art of the critics of the court)
content.power: the Salon exhibitions in Paris made art public and political
content.individual: the hero who sacrifices himself for principle
content.others: Greece and Rome held up as mirrors
content.read: A society whose art told it to sacrifice for ideas: a warning sign of revolution.

content.name: Nineteenth-century Britain
content.fears: revolution, the loss of the old countryside
content.power: public galleries and a middle class buying art
content.individual: the Romantic artist and the sublime
content.others: an empire shown through trade and exploration
content.read: Stable institutions that adapted rather than broke; awe of nature and of progress.

content.name: Nineteenth-century America
content.honours: the land, independence, the common man, Manifest Destiny
content.fears: losing the wilderness and the founding ideals; division (the Civil War)
content.power: national legends in history painting; landscapes as national pride
content.others: Native Americans often shown as part of a vanishing past
content.read: A young nation building its myths as it grew; land and liberty as its rallying ideas.

content.name: Modern Paris
content.honours: modern life, leisure, light, individual vision
content.power: dealers and buyers instead of church and king
content.individual: the artist as an independent voice
content.others: Japanese prints changed how Europe composed pictures
content.read: Power spread out among many: markets, critics and the public.

items.title: LENS_QUESTIONS: How do they show power?
LENS_QUESTIONS: How do they show other peoples?
items.content: How do they show other peoples?

items.title: SYMBOLS: Skull
content: Memento mori: remember you will die. A warning against vanity.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Snuffed candle
content: A life that has ended, or how short life is.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Soap bubbles
content: Life is as fragile as a bubble (homo bulla).

items.title: SYMBOLS: White lily
content: Purity; in religious art, the Virgin Mary.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Dog
content: Loyalty and faithfulness (in marriage portraits, or at a knight’s feet on tombs).

items.title: SYMBOLS: Lamb
content: Innocence and sacrifice; in Christian art, Christ.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Dove
content: Peace; in Christian art, the Holy Spirit.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Apple
content: Temptation and the Fall; in Greek myth, the golden apple of discord.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Grapes and wine
content: Celebration, or in religious art the wine of the Eucharist.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Pearls
content: Wealth and purity, but also vanity in Dutch art.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Lute and instruments
content: Harmony, love, or passing pleasures (music fades).

items.title: SYMBOLS: Letter
content: News from someone absent: love, business or a secret.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Map or globe
content: Knowledge, trade, empire, the wider world.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Books
content: Learning and wisdom, or the vanity of knowledge.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Owl
content: Wisdom (bird of Athena, on Athenian coins).

items.title: SYMBOLS: Eagle
content: Empire and supreme power (Zeus/Jupiter, Roman legions, later many states).

items.title: SYMBOLS: Lion
content: Royal power, courage; a hunted lion shows the king’s strength.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Horse
content: Power, nobility, war; a rearing horse shows a ruler’s command.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Crown, sceptre and orb
content: Royal authority; the orb is rule over the world.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Keys
content: Authority to open and close (in Christian art, St Peter).

items.title: SYMBOLS: Scallop shell
content: Pilgrimage (to Santiago de Compostela); in Venus scenes, birth from the sea.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Ultramarine blue
content: Made from lapis lazuli from Afghanistan; dearer than gold, so used for the most important figure or by painters showing off a patron’s money.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Purple
content: Imperial power: Tyrian purple dye was extremely costly.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Gold leaf / gold ground
content: Heaven, holiness and eternity, a light that never changes.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Black clothes
content: In the Dutch Republic and Spain black dye was expensive: sober but wealthy.

items.title: SYMBOLS: White linen
content: Cleanliness, purity and a well-kept house.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Open window
content: The link between home and the world; light as clarity.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Gold chain
content: A gift from a ruler: favour, fame, and being bound to power.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Classical bust
content: Respect for the ancients and their wisdom.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Finger pointing up
content: Heaven, higher truth, or an idea above earthly things.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Broken or cast-off chains
content: Freedom, or freedom of the mind over the body.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Columns and arches
content: Order, Rome, law and civic virtue.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Ruins
content: The passing of empires and time.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Storm, sea, mountains
content: The Sublime: nature’s power, awe and terror.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Cypress
content: Death and eternity; planted in cemeteries.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Wheat and harvest
content: The cycle of life and the year; bread and survival.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Umbrella, top hat
content: The modern middle class in the city.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Flag
content: The nation; who controls the flag controls the story.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Mount Fuji
content: Permanence, the sacred centre of Japan, immortality.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Prussian blue
content: A synthetic blue imported into Japan from about 1820: a modern novelty.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Boats in danger
content: Human effort and teamwork against nature.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Pine, bamboo and plum
content: The "three friends of winter": endurance, integrity and renewal.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Dragon
content: Imperial power and the forces of water and weather (good, not evil, in China).

items.title: SYMBOLS: Carp
content: Perseverance (the carp that leaps the falls becomes a dragon).

items.title: SYMBOLS: Red seals on a painting
content: Each owner or emperor stamped it: a record of who admired it.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Lotus
content: Rebirth (it rises clean from mud); in Egypt, creation and the sun.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Blue-green faience
content: The colour of the Nile, plants and new life.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Hippopotamus
content: A dangerous river animal: chaos, made safe in art.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Lamassu (winged bull or lion with a man’s head)
content: Lamassu (winged bull or lion with a man’s head)
Guardian of palace gates, power of the king.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Five legs
content: So the guardian looks complete from front and side.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Left foot forward
content: An Egyptian convention adopted by early Greek sculptors.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Archaic smile
content: A sign of life and well-being in early Greek sculpture.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Contrapposto
content: Weight on one leg: the body looks alive and relaxed.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Monkey
content: Foolishness, vanity or lust in European art.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Fire
content: Destruction and change, or the Sublime.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Crowd watching
content: The public as witnesses of history.

items.title: SYMBOLS: The painter in the picture
SYMBOLS: Distant church
content: Faith in the background of daily life.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Swirling sky
content: Nature full of energy (and the painter’s inner life).

items.title: SYMBOLS: Lace collar
content: Status and wealth: lace was hand-made and costly.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Direct gaze
content: The sitter meets you as an equal.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Chained animal
content: Wildness tied and tamed; also mystery.

items.title: SYMBOLS: Dugout canoe
content: The frontier and the river as road.

items.title: WORDS: amen
content: Latin/Greek amen < Hebrew amen "truly, so be it" (root a-m-n, "firm, faithful")
Said the same way in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Arabic (amin) and English.

items.title: WORDS: hallelujah
content: Hebrew hallelu-yah "praise (you all) Yah", Yah being short for the divine name
Appears 24 times in the Psalms; the Greek form alleluia is in Revelation 19.

items.title: WORDS: jubilee
content: Old French jubile < Late Latin jubilaeus < Hebrew yovel "ram's horn"
The ram's horn announced the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25); Latin jubilare "to shout" helped the spelling.

items.title: WORDS: sabbath
content: Old English sabat < Latin sabbatum < Greek sabbaton < Hebrew shabbat "rest", from shavat "to stop"
Many languages name Saturday after it: Spanish sabado, Italian sabato, Russian subbota.

items.title: WORDS: cherub
content: Latin cherub < Greek cheroub < Hebrew kerub (plural kerubim)
Probably related to Akkadian karibu "one who blesses"; the chubby-baby look came from Renaissance art.

items.title: WORDS: seraph
content: The same root names the "fiery serpents" of Numbers 21.

items.title: WORDS: messiah
content: Hebrew mashiach "anointed one" (Greek christos is the translation of the same word)
So "Messiah" and "Christ" mean the same thing, one from Hebrew and one from Greek.

items.title: WORDS: satan
content: Hebrew satan "adversary, accuser" (from a verb "to oppose")
In Job and Zechariah it is "the satan", a title, before it became a name.

items.title: WORDS: behemoth
content: Hebrew behemot, plural of behemah "beast" (a plural of majesty: "the great beast")
From Job 40; now any huge thing.

items.title: WORDS: leviathan
content: Hebrew livyatan, probably from a root "to twist, coil"
A sea monster in Job 41 and Psalm 74; it has a cousin Lotan in the Ugaritic myths.

items.title: WORDS: shibboleth
content: In Judges 12 the Ephraimites could not say "sh", so the word became a test; now a password or slogan.

items.title: WORDS: scapegoat
content: English "escape goat", William Tyndale's 1530 translation of Hebrew azazel (Leviticus 16)
Tyndale read azazel as ez ozel "the goat that departs"; many scholars think Azazel is a name.

items.title: WORDS: abba
content: Jesus uses it in Mark 14:36; Paul in Romans 8:15.

items.title: WORDS: rabbi
content: Rabboni in John 20:16 is a more intimate form.

items.title: WORDS: cinnamon
content: Greek kinnamomon, from a Semitic word (Hebrew qinnamon, Exodus 30:23)
The Greeks got the spice and the word through Phoenician traders.

items.title: WORDS: sack
content: Old English sacc < Latin saccus < Greek sakkos < Semitic (Hebrew saq "sackcloth")
One of the oldest trade words: it travelled from Hebrew to Greek to Latin to English.

items.title: WORDS: bible
content: Old French bible < Medieval Latin biblia < Greek ta biblia "the books" < byblos "papyrus"
Byblos was the Phoenician port that exported papyrus to Greece, so the Bible is named after a city.

items.title: WORDS: angel
content: Old English engel and Old French angele < Latin angelus < Greek angelos "messenger"
Translates Hebrew mal'akh, which also just means "messenger".

items.title: WORDS: apostle
content: Greek apostolos "one sent out" < apo "away" + stellein "to send"

items.title: WORDS: baptize
content: Greek baptizein "to dip, immerse" < baptein "to dip"
Used of dyeing cloth as well.

items.title: WORDS: church
content: Old English cirice < Greek kyriakon (doma) "the Lord's (house)" < kyrios "lord"
Romance languages took Greek ekklesia "assembly" instead: French eglise, Spanish iglesia.

items.title: WORDS: bishop
content: Old English biscop < Latin episcopus < Greek episkopos "overseer"
Worn down over centuries: e-PISCOP-us became biscop.

items.title: WORDS: history
content: Latin historia < Greek historia "inquiry, finding out by asking" < histor "wise man, witness"
Herodotus called his book Historiai, "Inquiries". "Story" is the same word worn down.

items.title: WORDS: democracy
content: First used in Athens in the 400s BC.

items.title: WORDS: tyrant
content: Greek tyrannos "ruler who seized power", probably from a language of Asia Minor (Lydian?)
At first it was not an insult: it only meant a ruler without inherited right.

items.title: WORDS: alphabet
content: Latin alphabetum < Greek alpha + beta < Phoenician aleph "ox" + bet "house"
See Research → Learn → Alphabets for every letter's story.

items.title: WORDS: academy
content: Greek Akademeia, the olive grove of the hero Akademos outside Athens where Plato taught

items.title: WORDS: marathon
content: Greek Marathon, the plain where Athens beat Persia in 490 BC; the name means "fennel field"
The 26-mile race was invented for the 1896 Olympics from the legend of the runner Pheidippides.

items.title: WORDS: panic
content: Greek panikon "of Pan", the wild god whose shout was said to scatter armies in sudden fear

items.title: WORDS: cemetery
content: Late Latin coemeterium < Greek koimeterion "sleeping place" < koiman "to put to sleep"
An early Christian word: the dead are "asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4).

items.title: WORDS: idiot
content: Latin idiota < Greek idiotes "private person, layman" < idios "one's own"
In Athens it meant a citizen who took no part in public life.

items.title: WORDS: school
content: Old English scol < Latin schola < Greek schole "leisure", then "what you do with leisure: discussion"

items.title: WORDS: cipher
content: Old French cifre < Medieval Latin cifra < Arabic sifr "zero, empty"
Zero was so strange to Europeans that its name came to mean a secret code (and "decipher").

items.title: WORDS: cryptography
content: Same root as "crypt", a hidden vault.

items.title: WORDS: planet
content: Planets wander against the fixed stars.

items.title: WORDS: atom
content: Latin atomus < Greek atomos "uncuttable" (a- "not" + temnein "to cut")
Democritus' idea of the smallest piece; ironically atoms can be split.

items.title: WORDS: music
content: Latin musica < Greek mousike (techne) "art of the Muses"

items.title: WORDS: Europe
content: Greek Europe, a Phoenician princess carried off by Zeus; the name may come from a Semitic word "evening, west" (Akkadian erebu "to set")
The Semitic origin is a theory, not certain.

items.title: WORDS: salary
content: Probably an allowance connected with salt; the story that soldiers were "paid in salt" is not proven.

items.title: WORDS: candidate
content: Latin candidatus "dressed in white" < candidus "shining white"
Romans running for office wore a whitened toga.

items.title: WORDS: senate
content: A council of elders; "senior" and "senile" are relatives.

items.title: WORDS: emperor
content: Old French empereor < Latin imperator "commander" < imperare "to command"
A title soldiers shouted for a victorious general before it meant a monarch.

items.title: WORDS: legion
content: A legion was a "levy", a chosen body of men.

items.title: WORDS: Caesar
content: Latin Caesar, the family name of Julius Caesar
Became a title: German Kaiser, Russian tsar.

items.title: WORDS: palace
content: Old French palais < Latin Palatium, the Palatine Hill in Rome where Augustus lived

items.title: WORDS: August
content: Latin Augustus, renamed in 8 BC for the emperor; the month was Sextilis "sixth"
July is named for Julius Caesar (formerly Quintilis "fifth").

items.title: WORDS: September
content: It was the 7th month when the Roman year began in March; so October 8, November 9, December 10.

items.title: WORDS: January
content: Latin Ianuarius, the month of Janus, two-faced god of doors and beginnings

items.title: WORDS: quarantine
content: Ships from plague ports waited forty days before landing.

items.title: WORDS: decimate
content: Latin decimare "to take one in ten" < decem "ten"
A Roman punishment: a mutinous unit drew lots and every tenth man was killed by his comrades.

items.title: WORDS: trivia
content: Latin trivium "place where three roads meet" (tri- + via)
Things you would hear at a crossroads, common gossip.

items.title: WORDS: companion
content: Old French compaignon < Late Latin companio "one who shares bread" < com- + panis "bread"

items.title: WORDS: sinister
content: The left side was thought unlucky by omen-readers.

items.title: WORDS: muscle
content: A flexing muscle looked like a mouse moving under the skin.

items.title: WORDS: verse
content: Latin versus "a turning (of the plough), a line" < vertere "to turn"
The Bible was divided into numbered verses by Robert Estienne in 1551.

items.title: WORDS: crusade
content: French croisade and Spanish cruzada < Latin crux "cross"

items.title: WORDS: pagan
content: Christianity spread first in cities, so country people kept the old gods longest (one leading theory).

items.title: WORDS: vandal
content: The Vandals, a Germanic people who sacked Rome in AD 455
The word "vandalism" was coined in 1794 by Abbe Gregoire about damage in the French Revolution.

items.title: WORDS: mile
content: Old English mil < Latin milia passuum "a thousand paces"
A Roman pace was two steps.

items.title: WORDS: sky
content: English already had "heaven"; the Vikings gave "sky".

items.title: WORDS: law
content: Old English lagu < Old Norse log "something laid down"
The Danelaw was the area under Danish law.

items.title: WORDS: they
content: Even pronouns came from the Vikings: they, them, their.

items.title: WORDS: berserk
content: Warriors who fought in a trance-like fury.

items.title: WORDS: ransack
content: Old Norse rannsaka "to search a house" (rann "house" + saka "to seek")

items.title: WORDS: Thursday
content: Old English thunresdaeg "Thor's day" (with Norse influence)
Tuesday is Tiw's (Tyr's) day, Wednesday Woden's (Odin's), Friday Frigg's.

items.title: WORDS: egg
content: Old Norse egg (Old English had ey, plural eyren)
Printer William Caxton (1490) told of a merchant who asked for "eggys" and was told the woman spoke no French: she said "eyren".

items.title: WORDS: beef
content: After 1066 English peasants kept the animal (cow, ox) and Norman lords ate the meat (beef); likewise pig/pork, sheep/mutton.

items.title: WORDS: government
content: Old French governement < Latin gubernare "to steer" < Greek kybernan "to steer a ship"
"Cybernetics" comes from the same Greek verb.

items.title: WORDS: parliament
content: Old French parlement "a speaking, a conference" < parler "to speak"

items.title: WORDS: curfew
content: A bell told people to cover their hearths at night.

items.title: WORDS: mortgage
content: The deal "dies" when the debt is paid, or the land is lost.

items.title: WORDS: checkmate
content: Old French eschec mat < Persian shah mat "the king is helpless (or dead)"

items.title: WORDS: algebra
content: Medieval Latin < Arabic al-jabr "the restoring (of broken parts)"
From the title of al-Khwarizmi's book (c. 820); "algorithm" comes from his own name.

items.title: WORDS: algorithm
content: Medieval Latin algorismus < al-Khwarizmi, the Persian mathematician in Baghdad

items.title: WORDS: zero
content: Italian zefiro < Medieval Latin zephirum < Arabic sifr "empty" (a translation of Sanskrit shunya)

items.title: WORDS: admiral
content: Old French amiral < Arabic amir al- "commander of the ..."
The d crept in from Latin admirari.

items.title: WORDS: alchemy
content: Old French alquemie < Arabic al-kimiya < Greek khemeia (perhaps from Kemet, Egypt's own name)

items.title: WORDS: coffee
content: Italian caffe < Turkish kahve < Arabic qahwa
Possibly linked to Kaffa in Ethiopia.

items.title: WORDS: sugar
content: Old French sukere < Medieval Latin succarum < Arabic sukkar < Persian shakar < Sanskrit sharkara "grit, gravel"
A word that crossed four language families.

items.title: WORDS: assassin
content: A name given to the Nizari Ismaili order of the Crusader era; the claim they used hashish is probably a hostile rumour.

items.title: WORDS: magazine
content: French magasin < Italian magazzino < Arabic makhazin "storehouses"
A gun magazine stores bullets; a printed magazine is a storehouse of articles.

items.title: WORDS: paradise
content: Old French paradis < Latin paradisus < Greek paradeisos < Old Persian paridaida "walled enclosure"
A Persian royal park; the Septuagint used it for the Garden of Eden.

items.title: WORDS: magic
content: Old French magique < Latin magicus < Greek magikos < magos < Old Persian magush "priest"
The magi of Matthew 2 were such priests or astrologers.

items.title: WORDS: jungle
content: Hindi jangal < Sanskrit jangala "dry, arid land"
The meaning flipped from dry land to thick forest.

items.title: WORDS: avatar
content: Sanskrit avatara "descent" (of a god to earth)

items.title: WORDS: typhoon
content: Arabic tufan and Chinese tai fung "great wind", mixed with Greek Typhon the storm monster

items.title: WORDS: tea
content: Languages that got tea by sea say "te"; by land, from Mandarin cha, they say "chai/chay".

items.title: WORDS: tycoon
content: Japanese taikun "great lord", a title used for the shogun with foreigners

items.title: WORDS: chocolate
content: Spanish chocolate < Nahuatl (Aztec) xocolatl, probably "bitter water"

items.title: WORDS: canoe
content: One of the first American words Columbus wrote down (1492).

items.title: WORDS: banana
content: Portuguese/Spanish < a West African language (Wolof banaana)

items.title: WORDS: goodbye
content: "Good" replaced "God" by analogy with good day, good night.

items.title: WORDS: nice
content: Old French nice "silly, simple" < Latin nescius "ignorant" (ne "not" + scire "know")
Over 700 years it meant foolish, shy, fussy, precise, then pleasant.

items.title: WORDS: bedlam
content: The Hospital of St Mary of Bethlehem in London, an asylum

items.title: WORDS: nightmare
content: Old English mare, a goblin believed to sit on sleepers' chests

items.title: WORDS: clue
content: Theseus followed a clew of thread out of the Labyrinth.

items.title: WORDS: deadline
content: American Civil War prison camps: a line prisoners were shot for crossing
Later used by printers, then for any time limit.

items.title: WORDS: robot
content: Czech robota "forced labour", from Karel Capek's play R.U.R. (1920)

items.title: WORDS: quiz
content: The story that a Dublin theatre owner invented it for a bet is a myth.

items.title: MYTHS: posh
content: Not "Port Out, Starboard Home" (no ticket ever printed it). Origin unknown; maybe old slang "posh" meaning money or a dandy.

items.title: MYTHS: news
content: Not North-East-West-South: it is just the plural of "new" (new things), like French nouvelles.

items.title: MYTHS: sincere
content: Not Latin sine cera "without wax" for honest statues; it is from Latin sincerus "pure, whole".

items.title: MYTHS: golf
content: Not "Gentlemen Only, Ladies Forbidden"; probably from Dutch kolf "club". Acronym words are almost all 20th century.

items.title: MYTHS: SOS
content: Not "Save Our Souls"; chosen in 1906 because · · · — — — · · · is easy to send and recognise.

items.title: MYTHS: rule of thumb
content: No law ever let a man beat his wife with a stick no thicker than his thumb; the phrase is about rough measuring with the thumb.

items.title: MYTHS: OK
content: Most likely "oll korrect", a joke misspelling in Boston newspapers in 1839, spread by the "Old Kinderhook" election club of Martin Van Buren in 1840.

items.title: MYTHS: salary
content: Roman soldiers being "paid in salt" is unproven; the link to salt is real but its meaning is unclear.

items.title: FAMILIES: Indo-European
content: About half the world speaks one; from PIE on the steppe (leading theory).

items.title: FAMILIES: Afro-Asiatic
content: North Africa and the Middle East.
Biblical, then Mishnaic, revived as Modern Hebrew
language of the Persian Empire and of Jesus; parts of Daniel and Ezra
hieroglyphs, then Coptic (still used in church)

items.title: FAMILIES: Austronesian
content: From Taiwan to Madagascar and Hawaii.

items.title: FAMILIES: Niger-Congo
content: The largest family by number of languages.

items.title: COGNATES: mother
content: English mother · German Mutter · Latin mater · Greek meter · Sanskrit matar · Irish mathair · Russian mat' · all < PIE *mehter

items.title: COGNATES: father
content: English father · German Vater · Latin pater · Greek pater · Sanskrit pitar · Gothic fadar · < PIE *ph2ter (Grimm's law turned p into f in Germanic)

items.title: COGNATES: three
content: English three · German drei · Latin tres · Greek treis · Sanskrit trayas · Russian tri · < PIE *treyes

items.title: COGNATES: night
content: English night · German Nacht · Latin nox/noctis · Greek nyx/nyktos · Sanskrit nakta · Lithuanian naktis · < PIE *nekwts

items.title: COGNATES: peace
content: Hebrew shalom · Arabic salam · Aramaic shlama · Akkadian shalamu "to be whole" · < Semitic root sh-l-m

items.title: COGNATES: king
content: Latin rex · Sanskrit raj(a) · Irish ri · Gaulish -rix (Vercingetorix) · < PIE *h3reg- "to rule"; English king is Germanic (*kuningaz)

items.title: HEBREW: ב
content: b, or v without the dot

items.title: HEBREW: כ
content: k, or kh without the dot

items.title: HEBREW: פ
content: p, or f without the dot

items.title: GREEK: Σ
content: s (ς at the end of a word)

content.title: Abraham's journey
stops: Terah's family leaves Ur of the Chaldeans (Genesis 11:31).
They settle in Haran; Abram is called to go on (Genesis 12:1-4).
At the oak of Moreh God promises the land; Abram builds an altar.
Another altar between Bethel and Ai.
A famine drives him to Egypt.
He settles by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron.

content.title: The Exodus
stops: Israel leaves Rameses (Exodus 12:37); the site is usually placed at Qantir.
First camp (Tell el-Maskhuta is the usual guess).
The sea divides (Exodus 14). Where is debated: the Gulf of Suez, the Bitter Lakes or a northern lake.
The Law is given. Jebel Musa is the traditional site; others are proposed.
The spies are sent; Israel stays in the wilderness forty years.
Moses sees the land and dies (Deuteronomy 34).
Joshua leads Israel across the Jordan.

content.title: Into exile in Babylon
stops: Nebuchadnezzar takes the city; the Temple is burned in 586 BC.
King Zedekiah is judged at Nebuchadnezzar's headquarters.
The road follows the Euphrates (where Babylon beat Egypt in 605 BC).
The exiles settle by the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137).

content.title: Alexander's march
stops: First victory over the Persian satraps.
Seven-month siege of the island city.
The oracle of Amun calls him son of the god.
The decisive victory over Darius (331 BC).
Hard years of war in Bactria.
Samarkand; he kills his friend Cleitus in a drunken quarrel.
Victory over King Porus and his elephants (326 BC); the army refuses to go on.
Down the Indus to the sea.
He dies in Babylon in June 323 BC, aged 32.

content.title: Hannibal's march on Rome
stops: Hannibal sets out from Spain with about 40,000 men and 37 elephants.
He crosses the river that Rome had set as a boundary.

content.title: Laws of Hammurabi
content.why: One of the oldest law collections, carved on a black stone stele now in the Louvre. About 280 laws on trade, family, property and injury, framed by a prologue saying the gods chose Hammurabi to bring justice.
look: "Eye for an eye" (laws 196–200) and how punishment depends on social class
Laws on builders, doctors and boatmen: early consumer protection
Compare with the Covenant Code in Exodus 21–23

content.title: The Ten Commandments
content.why: The core of Israel's covenant law, given at Sinai in the biblical account; Jews and Christians number the ten slightly differently. Unlike Hammurabi, the laws speak directly to "you" and begin with God, not the king.
look: The Sabbath reason in Exodus 20:11 (creation) versus Deuteronomy 5:15 (Egypt)
Commands about thoughts ("covet"), not only acts

content.title: The Shema
content.why: "Hear, O Israel": the central Jewish confession of one God, said morning and evening; Jesus called it the first commandment (Mark 12:29).

content.title: The Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone)
text: The Inscription on the Stele of Méšaʿ/Translation
content.why: King Mesha boasts of throwing off Israel's rule after the death of Omri's son; the same revolt is told from Israel's side in 2 Kings 3. It names Omri, the God of Israel (YHWH) and probably the "House of David".
look: Compare with 2 Kings 3
Mesha credits his god Chemosh much as Israel credits YHWH

content.title: The Siloam Inscription
content.why: Carved where two tunnelling teams met under Jerusalem, in the water tunnel of 2 Kings 20:20. One of the oldest Hebrew inscriptions.
look: How the teams heard each other's picks through the rock

content.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
content.why: Cyrus' account of taking Babylon, presenting himself as chosen by Marduk and returning captive peoples and their gods to their homes, which matches the decree for the Jews in Ezra 1.
look: Compare with Ezra 1:1–4 and Isaiah 45:1
Royal propaganda: the old king is blamed for everything

content.title: The Behistun Inscription
text: The Sculptures and Inscription of Darius the Great on the Rock of Behistûn in Persia/The Persian Text
content.why: Darius' account of how he took the throne, carved high on a cliff in three languages; it was the key to reading cuneiform, as the Rosetta Stone was for hieroglyphs.
look: The rebels Darius lists and his "the Lie" theme
Whether his story of the false Smerdis is true is debated

content.title: Pericles' Funeral Oration

What Tacitus thinks of the Christians, and of Nero

content.why: A peace treaty forced on King John that put the king under the law. Annulled within weeks but reissued, and later treated as the root of rights such as trial by jury.
look: Clauses 39 and 40: no free man punished "except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land"; justice not to be sold
Clause 61, the committee of 25 barons

content.title: The Mayflower Compact

content.title: The great flood
tellings: God sends a flood on a violent world but warns righteous Noah, who builds an ark for his family and pairs of animals. Afterwards Noah sends a raven and a dove, offers a sacrifice, and God sets the rainbow as a covenant never to flood the earth again.
Epic of Gilgamesh, tablet XI (and the older Atrahasis)

The gods decide to wipe out humanity (in Atrahasis because people are too noisy). The god Ea warns Utnapishtim, who builds a huge boat; it lands on Mount Nimush; he sends out a dove, a swallow and a raven, and sacrifices. The gods gather "like flies" at the smell and Utnapishtim is made immortal.
Zeus floods the world for its wickedness. Deucalion and Pyrrha survive in a chest and land on Mount Parnassus, then make new people by throwing stones over their shoulders.
Shatapatha Brahmana; later the Matsya Purana
A small fish asks Manu to save it; it grows huge and warns him of a flood. Manu ties his boat to the fish's horn and is towed to a northern mountain; he then begins humanity again.
The prophet Nuh preaches for many years and is mocked; he builds the ark by God's command. One of his sons refuses to board and drowns; the ark rests on Mount Judi.
The Book of Documents (Shujing) and later tales
A long flood is not a punishment to escape but a disaster to fix: Gun fails to dam it; his son Yu the Great spends 13 years digging channels and founds the Xia dynasty.
content.shared: A divine decision, one family warned, a boat, a mountain landing, birds sent out (Bible and Gilgamesh), a sacrifice and a new start for humanity.
content.differs: Why the flood comes (sin, noise, divine whim), whether the hero becomes immortal, one God or many, and whether the flood is escaped (Noah, Manu) or tamed (Yu).
content.scholars: The Bible and Gilgamesh accounts are so close in details (the birds, the sacrifice) that most scholars think they share a common Mesopotamian tradition; some link it to real river floods (a flood layer at Shuruppak, c. 2900 BC). Believers read Genesis as the true account that others remembered in distorted form. Flood stories in very distant places (China, the Americas) are usually explained as independent memories of local floods.

content.title: Creation of the world
tellings: One God speaks the world into order in six days, from light to humans "in his image", and rests on the seventh. The deep and the sea are simply created things, not rival gods.

The gods are born from the mingling of fresh water (Apsu) and salt water (Tiamat). Marduk defeats Tiamat, splits her body to make sky and earth, and makes humans from the blood of a rebel god so that the gods can rest.
Atum rises on a mound from the waters of Nun and creates Shu (air) and Tefnut (moisture); their children are Geb (earth) and Nut (sky). In Memphis, Ptah creates by thought and word.
First Chaos, then Gaia (Earth), Tartarus and Eros. Gaia bears Uranus (Sky); generations of gods overthrow one another until Zeus rules.
In the gap Ginnungagap, ice meets fire and the giant Ymir forms. Odin and his brothers kill Ymir and make the earth from his flesh, the sea from his blood and the sky from his skull.
The Creation Hymn wonders whether anyone knows how it began, "perhaps even he does not know". Another hymn makes the world from the sacrifice of the cosmic man, Purusha.
Pangu grows inside a cosmic egg for 18,000 years and pushes heaven and earth apart; when he dies his body becomes mountains, rivers and stars.
God created the heavens and the earth in six days (periods), which were "joined together" and then split; he is never tired by it (50:38).
content.shared: Order out of water or chaos, sky separated from earth, a sequence of stages, and humans made last or for a purpose.
content.differs: Creation by word (Genesis, Ptah) or by combat and a body cut apart (Enuma Elish, Ymir, Pangu); one God or generations of gods; humans as image-bearers or as servants who do the gods' work.
content.scholars: Many scholars read Genesis 1 as deliberately answering Babylonian myth: the sea monsters are mere creatures and the sun and moon are just "lamps". Others stress how different its single, unopposed Creator is. Genesis 1 and 2 are read by some as two sources, by others as one account from two angles.

content.title: People made from clay
tellings: God forms the man from the dust of the ground and breathes the breath of life into his nostrils (Adam, from adamah "ground").
The mother goddess mixes clay with the flesh and blood of a slain god to make humans to do the gods' labour.
The ram-headed god Khnum shapes each child on his potter's wheel.
Prometheus shapes humans from earth and water and steals fire for them.
The goddess Nüwa models people from yellow earth; tired, she drags a rope through mud and the drops become ordinary people.
God created the human from clay, "from an extract of clay".
content.shared: A craftsman deity, earth or clay, and something extra (breath, divine blood, fire) that makes the figure alive.
content.differs: The purpose: fellowship and stewardship (Genesis), forced labour (Atrahasis), or no reason given.
content.scholars: Pottery was everywhere in the ancient world, so it was a natural picture of making; whether the shared image comes from contact or from common experience is open.

items.title: MYTHS: The tower and the languages

content.title: The tower and the languages
tellings: One-language humanity builds a city and a tower "with its top in the heavens" at Babel; God confuses their speech and scatters them.
Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
A passage (the "spell of Nudimmud") speaks of a time when all peoples spoke to Enlil in one tongue until Enki changed their speech; how to translate it is debated.
Babylon's ziggurat Etemenanki, "House of the foundation of heaven and earth", was a real stepped tower about 90 m high.
Diego Duran (1580s), the Great Pyramid of Cholula
After the conquest Duran recorded a tale of giants who built a tower to reach the sky and were scattered; Spanish influence is likely.
content.shared: Human pride, a tower or mountain to heaven, and the origin of many languages.
content.differs: Only Genesis joins the tower and the confusion of languages into one judgement story.
content.scholars: Most link Babel to Babylon's ziggurats; the story also plays on the name (Babel and Hebrew balal "confuse").

items.title: MYTHS: The baby saved from the water

content.title: The baby saved from the water
tellings: To escape Pharaoh's order, Moses' mother hides him in a papyrus basket sealed with pitch on the Nile; Pharaoh's daughter finds and adopts him.
Sargon's mother, a priestess, sets him in a reed basket sealed with bitumen on the Euphrates; a water-drawer finds him and he becomes king.
Romulus and Remus are set adrift on the Tiber, nursed by a she-wolf and raised by a shepherd; Romulus founds Rome.
Kunti puts her baby Karna in a basket on the river; a charioteer's family raises him.
Danae and baby Perseus are shut in a chest and cast into the sea; they wash up on Seriphos.
content.shared: A threatened baby, a basket or chest on water, rescue by a stranger and a great future.
content.differs: Moses is rescued to deliver an enslaved people, not to found an empire; Sargon's story is told by himself as a king's legitimacy tale.
content.scholars: Folklorists call it the "exposed hero" pattern. The Sargon text is earlier than the written Exodus in the view of most scholars, though its copy is from the 700s BC; others see it as a common motif, not a borrowing.

items.title: MYTHS: The god who fights the sea dragon

content.title: The god who fights the sea dragon
tellings: Marduk slays Tiamat, the sea, and builds the world from her body.
Baal defeats Yam (Sea) and the seven-headed serpent Lotan.
Poems praise God for crushing the heads of Leviathan and cutting Rahab; in Genesis 1 the sea is calm and obeys.
Zeus defeats Typhon, a monster of a hundred serpent heads.
Thor and the world serpent Jormungandr: they kill each other at Ragnarok.
Indra kills the serpent Vritra and releases the rivers.
content.shared: The storm or sky god against chaos, often the sea, often many-headed; victory brings order and kingship.
content.differs: In most, the fight creates the world; in the Bible it is poetry about God's power over chaos, not a creation battle in Genesis.
content.scholars: The Ugaritic texts (found 1929) showed that Leviathan/Lotan was a known Canaanite figure, so biblical poets used a familiar image.

items.title: MYTHS: The land of the dead

content.title: The land of the dead
tellings: The heart of the dead is weighed against the feather of Maat (truth); the good go on to the Field of Reeds, the heart of the wicked is eaten by Ammit.
A "house of dust" where the dead eat clay and wear feathers; much the same for everyone.
Sheol, the shadowy grave; later texts speak of resurrection, "some to everlasting life, some to shame".
Hades: pale shades without strength; a few heroes in Elysium, a few sinners punished in Tartarus.
Warriors chosen by the Valkyries go to Valhalla or Folkvangr; many others go to Hel.
Resurrection of the body and judgement, with eternal life with God (heaven/Jannah) or separation (hell/Jahannam).
content.shared: A place below, a crossing (a river, a boatman), and a growing idea of judgement.
content.differs: A gloomy fate for all (Mesopotamia, early Sheol, Homer) versus moral judgement (Egypt) and bodily resurrection (later Judaism, Christianity, Islam).
content.scholars: Historians trace how ideas of afterlife and judgement developed and influenced each other; believers read the later revelation as fuller truth rather than borrowing.

items.title: MYTHS: The end of the world

content.title: The end of the world
tellings: Ragnarok: a great winter, the gods die fighting the giants and monsters, the world sinks and then rises green again.
A saviour (Saoshyant) comes, the dead rise, a river of molten metal purifies all and evil is destroyed (Frashokereti).
Christ returns, Satan is defeated, the dead are judged and God makes "a new heaven and a new earth".
The Hour: the sky splits, the mountains are like wool, every soul is judged by its deeds.
Time runs in vast cycles; at the end of the age (Kali Yuga) Kalki comes and the world is dissolved and recreated.
We live in the Fifth Sun, which will end in earthquakes as four suns ended before.
content.shared: Cosmic catastrophe, a final battle, judgement or renewal.
content.differs: A straight line to a final new creation (Zoroastrianism, Christianity, Islam) or endless cycles (India, Aztecs, partly Norse).
content.scholars: Many historians think Persian ideas of resurrection and a final judgement influenced later Jewish thought after the exile; others argue the roots are already in the Hebrew prophets.
